article.headline: Vitalik Buterin Makes the Case for a Sovereign Local AI Stack
article.lede: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin published a detailed account of the AI stack he runs entirely on local hardware — no cloud dependencies, no third-party data exposure, no outbound messages or crypto transactions without explicit human sign-off. The impetus is a security landscape around agentic AI that he considers dangerously cavalier, illustrated at length by vulnerabilities accumulating around OpenClaw, the fastest-growing GitHub repository in history.
article.body:
The catalyst is **OpenClaw**, an agentic AI framework — meaning one where the AI autonomously uses hundreds of tools to complete tasks rather than simply answering questions. Cybersecurity firm Gen found roughly 15% of community-built skills on OpenClaw's ClawHub marketplace contained malicious instructions, some silently exfiltrating user data or deploying *reverse shells* (covert backdoors giving an attacker remote control). Researchers at Oasis Security found that any website a developer visits can silently take over a local OpenClaw instance through a WebSocket connection to localhost, with no plugins and no user interaction required. A Cisco audit found a third-party skill that invisibly routed user data to an external server via a curl command the user never saw.

Buterin's response is architectural. He runs all inference locally — no API calls to Anthropic, OpenAI, or any hosted service — using **Qwen3.5:35B**, a 35-billion-parameter open-weight model. His hardware is either an NVIDIA 5090 laptop or an AMD Ryzen AI Max Pro with 128GB unified memory, benchmarking at 90 and 51 tokens per second respectively. He sets a personal floor of 50 tok/sec: below that, the daily experience becomes too slow to tolerate. Notably, NVIDIA's own DGX Spark underperformed both machines despite heavy marketing.

The structural defense against *prompt injection* — attacks where malicious text embedded in a webpage or document instructs the agent to take unauthorized actions — is mandatory sandboxing via *bubblewrap*, a Linux containerization tool. Agents run in filesystem sandboxes that can only access whitelisted directories and network ports. A malicious website processed inside the sandbox cannot reach the wallet, the home directory, or system configuration. He chose *llama-server* over the more popular Ollama because it fits larger models into GPU memory and exposes a local HTTP endpoint compatible with any OpenAI-format client, including Claude Code.

At the action layer, a custom messaging daemon enforces explicit permissions. The LLM can message Buterin freely; messaging anyone else requires human confirmation. Crypto wallet transactions are fully gated. A 1TB local Wikipedia dump plus local manuals reduces the number of queries that must leave the machine at all — each external search request is a potential data leak. He flags the remaining gap: he wants someone to build a Tor-wrapped search skill for queries that still need to go out.

Buterin is candid about what the setup cannot yet do. Qwen3.5:35B one-shots simple apps and games reliably but struggles with domain-specific cryptographic implementations. He frames the post explicitly as a starting point, not a finished product, and warns against copying the techniques wholesale and assuming they are secure. The argument is ultimately structural: the shift from chatbots to autonomous agents is not reversible, and the choice is whether to build privacy and security in from the start or inherit an ecosystem where convenience was assumed to come first.

concepts.definition: AI systems that autonomously execute multi-step tasks using external tools — browsing the web, writing and running code, sending messages — rather than just responding to a single question. The distinction matters for security: a chatbot's blast radius is limited to the conversation window, while an agent can act on the real world without a human approving each step.

An attack in which malicious text embedded in content the AI reads — a webpage, email, or document — instructs the model to ignore its original instructions and take unauthorized actions. The AI cannot reliably distinguish legitimate instructions from injected ones, making any agent that reads untrusted external content potentially vulnerable.

A Linux containerization tool (bubblewrap) that creates a restricted filesystem and network environment. A process inside the sandbox can only access files and ports that have been explicitly whitelisted, so a compromised AI agent cannot reach sensitive directories, wallet keys, or arbitrary network destinations.

A network connection initiated from a victim's machine to an attacker's server, giving the attacker a remote command prompt. Unlike a conventional intrusion, the victim machine makes the outbound call, which bypasses many firewalls. In the OpenClaw context, malicious skills were found to deploy reverse shells silently during normal agent operation.

repos.summary: OpenClaw is an agentic AI framework that lets an LLM autonomously execute tasks using hundreds of community-built skills. It became the fastest-growing GitHub repository in history by early 2026 and sits at the center of Buterin's security critique: its ClawHub marketplace has been found to host malicious skills, and its architecture permits agents to modify their own system prompts without user confirmation.

article.fact_check: The description of OpenClaw as 'the fastest-growing GitHub repository in history' originates in Buterin's blog post and is repeated by secondary sources; no independent third-party ranking is cited in the available research. The claim may be accurate but should be treated as asserted rather than independently verified.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

poster_vitalikbuterin.blurb: Vitalik Buterin is the co-founder of Ethereum, the leading smart contract blockchain. He is a prominent figure in the crypto space, known for his deep technical insights and philosophical writings on decentralization, governance, and Ethereum's roadmap. His X account shares updates on Ethereum development, layer-2 scaling, and broader crypto ecosystem trends, with over 5 million followers.
poster_vitalikbuterin.credibility_note: As Ethereum's co-founder, Vitalik is highly credible on blockchain technology, though his views may reflect a pro-Ethereum bias. He has a strong track record of accurate technical predictions and transparent communication.
